items.followUp: State five important points of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model places electrons in permitted orbits around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits.
rubric.how: Award for the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus.

rubric.why: Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that each orbit has a fixed or definite energy.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the fixed energy of the orbits.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted orbits do not lose energy by radiation.
rubric.description: States that an electron does not radiate energy while in an allowed orbit.
rubric.how: Award for the stability of electrons in allowed orbits.

rubric.why: An electron must absorb energy to move to a higher energy state.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit.
rubric.how: Award for the absorption and upward transition.

rubric.why: An electron releases energy when it moves to a lower energy state.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it falls to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award for the emission and downward transition.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits, also called shells.
Each orbit has a definite, fixed energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in an allowed orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to jump from a lower orbit to a higher orbit.
An electron emits energy when it falls from a higher orbit to a lower orbit.

items.followUp: A sample contains 1.204×10²⁴ CO₂ molecules. Calculate the amount in moles and its mass.

rubric.why: The amount in moles is found by dividing the number of molecules by Avogadro’s constant.
rubric.description: Writes the relationship between molecule number and amount in moles.
rubric.how: Award for a correct formula for calculating moles.

rubric.why: The molecule count is half of Avogadro’s constant.
rubric.description: Calculates the amount of CO₂ as 0.50 mol.
rubric.how: Award for the correct amount in moles.

rubric.why: The mass is the amount in moles multiplied by the molar mass; CO₂ has a molar mass of 44 g mol⁻¹.
rubric.description: Uses the mass formula and the correct molar mass of CO₂.
rubric.how: Award for the formula and a correct molar mass, in either g mol⁻¹ or kg mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: Multiplying 0.50 mol by 0.044 kg mol⁻¹ gives 0.022 kg.
rubric.description: Calculates the mass as 0.022 kg, or 22 g.
rubric.how: Award for the correct mass with a unit.

modelAnswer: Given: number of CO₂ molecules, N = 3.01×10²³; Avogadro constant, Nₐ = 6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.
Molar mass of CO₂, M = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g mol⁻¹ = 0.044 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = N/Nₐ.
Substitution: n = (3.01×10²³ molecules)/(6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹) = 0.50 mol.
Formula: m = nM.
Substitution: m = (0.50 mol)(0.044 kg mol⁻¹) = 0.022 kg = 22 g.
Answer: The sample contains 0.50 mol of CO₂ and has a mass of 0.022 kg (22 g).

items.followUp: Define hydrogen bonding and describe two effects it has on the properties of water.

rubric.why: A complete definition identifies hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular attraction involving a highly electronegative atom.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen and a highly electronegative atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an intermolecular attraction and 1 mark for specifying the highly electronegative atom.

rubric.why: The hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom in a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.description: Explains the attraction to a lone pair on an atom in a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the lone-pair attraction between neighbouring molecules.

rubric.why: Extra energy is required to overcome hydrogen bonds when molecules separate.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding raises boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for the boiling-point effect.

accept: ice less dense than liquid water
rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding gives water distinctive physical properties.
rubric.description: Gives another valid effect, such as water’s high surface tension or ice being less dense than liquid water.
rubric.how: Award for one additional correct effect.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (usually F, O, or N) and a lone pair on an electronegative atom in a neighbouring molecule.
For example, hydrogen bonds form between water molecules.
Hydrogen bonding makes the boiling points of substances higher because extra energy is needed to separate their molecules.
It also gives water a high surface tension; hydrogen bonding makes ice less dense than liquid water.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how external pressure and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which vapour pressure equals atmospheric or external pressure.
rubric.how: Award for the equality of vapour pressure and external pressure.

rubric.why: A higher external pressure requires a higher temperature for the vapour pressure to match it.
rubric.description: Explains how a change in external pressure affects boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for the correct pressure relationship.

rubric.why: More energy is needed to overcome stronger attractions between molecules.
rubric.description: Explains that stronger intermolecular forces raise the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for the correct intermolecular-force relationship.

rubric.why: Non-volatile impurities generally raise a liquid’s boiling point.
rubric.description: Gives a further factor that raises boiling point: non-volatile impurities.
rubric.how: Award for naming the impurities and stating their effect.

modelAnswer: The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the external atmospheric pressure.
Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point; lowering the pressure lowers it.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise the boiling point because more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
Non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: A suspension has a non-uniform composition.
rubric.description: States that a suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award for identifying its heterogeneous nature.

rubric.why: Suspension particles are relatively large and can be seen.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles are large or visible to the naked eye.
rubric.how: Award for a correct statement about particle size or visibility.

rubric.why: Suspended particles settle out when the mixture is left standing.
rubric.description: States that the particles settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award for the settling characteristic.

rubric.why: Suspended particles can be removed from the mixture by filtration.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles can be separated by filtration.
rubric.how: Award for the filtration characteristic.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its particles are large enough to be visible to the naked eye.
The particles settle down when the suspension is left standing.
The suspended particles can be separated by filtration.
